result.reason: Letter A is clearer: it signposts the quarter's three developments as a numbered sequence instead of B's single dense block, defines TIPS in plain language, explains why the 24-month cash reserve exists, identifies the comparison index rather than saying only "the benchmark index," and tells Agnes explicitly that the fee change requires no action from her. A also orients the reader on accounts, strategy and period before presenting numbers, where B opens cold on a return figure. A's one clarity weakness is stacking four percentages plus a gross-of-fees figure in one paragraph; B is tidier there, but not enough to outweigh the rest. On tone, A better suits a 78-year-old recently widowed client receiving her first letter addressed to her alone: it offers an unpressured invitation to call just to talk things through and flags the large-print copy the tone notes specify, which B omits. B drifts institutional and mildly promotional ("our disciplined approach," "ensures that our services remain highly cost-effective for you"), framing the fee cut as a firm selling point, and its closing thanks are boilerplate. B also lacks A's letterhead and date block. Judgment is on clarity and tone only, not length or factual accuracy.
